issues.legal_issue: A donor’s reservation of lifetime use and income from immovable property does not invalidate a gift where the donor executes a registered and properly attested instrument transferring absolute ownership and the donee accepts the gift.
material_facts: The donor executed a registered gift deed attested by two witnesses in favour of the donee.
The courts below found that the donee accepted the gift, and that finding was not challenged.
The deed transferred absolute title to the donee but reserved to the donor the right to use the property and receive its income during her lifetime.
The donor’s challenges alleging fraud, misrepresentation and undue influence had been rejected by the courts below.
The appeal’s relevant contention was that the donor’s retention of use, income and possession made the gift invalid.
issues.conclusion: The gift was valid notwithstanding the donor’s reservation of lifetime use and income and the absence of a transfer of possession; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 122 and 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 require a voluntary gift of existing property, acceptance during the donor’s lifetime while capable of giving, and, for immovable property, a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor and attested by at least two witnesses; they do not require delivery of possession. Section 129 no longer saves Hindu or Buddhist rules from Chapter VII, and Section 6 permits transfer of property except as specified, with its personal-enjoyment restriction not applying merely because the donor reserves lifetime use. The Court agreed with K. Balakrishnan v. K. Kamalam, (2004) 1 SCC 581, that ownership may be gifted while possession and enjoyment are retained by the donor. Naramadaben Maganlal Thakker v. Pranjivandas Maganlal Thakker, (1997) 2 SCC 255, was distinguished because the gift there was conditional, had not been accepted, and did not transfer absolute ownership. The Court also relied on the interpretation of Section 123 in Lallu Singh v. Gur Narain, AIR 1922 All. 467, and approved the relevant approach in Revappa v. Madhava Rao, AIR 1960 Mysore 97, and Tirath Singh v. Manmohan Singh, AIR 1981 Punjab and Haryana 174.

rule.if: gift_validity_appeal and immovable_property_gift and registered_donor_signed_attested_instrument and donee_accepted_during_donor_lifetime and absolute_title_transferred and donor_reserved_lifetime_use and not possession_delivered

predicates.gift_validity_appeal: A party appealed from a decision concerning the validity of a gift of property.
predicates.immovable_property_gift: The disputed gift concerned immovable property.
predicates.registered_donor_signed_attested_instrum: The donor executed a registered instrument transferring the property and the instrument was attested by at least two witnesses.
predicates.donee_accepted_during_donor_lifetime: The donee accepted the gift while the donor was alive and capable of giving.
predicates.absolute_title_transferred: The instrument transferred absolute ownership of the property to the donee.
predicates.donor_reserved_lifetime_use: The donor reserved the right to use the property or receive its income during the donor’s lifetime.
predicates.possession_delivered: Possession of the gifted property was transferred to the donee.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns an immovable-property gift made by a registered, signed and attested instrument, accepted during the donor’s lifetime and transferring absolute title, the gift remains valid even if the donor reserves lifetime use and possession is not delivered.
